gate_reasoning: Stage 1 has produced a substantively well-structured analysis with good framework depth — the value chain mapping, solution profiling, and hypothesis testing are coherent and appropriately scoped. However, 73% of scored claims are Low confidence, driven predominantly by vendor-marketing-override (20 claims) and trade-press-only-override (12 claims). The three most load-bearing claims for the pain-point thesis — total North America freight fraud losses ($725M), nuclear verdict medians ($36M), and Indonesia truck fleet informality (75% single-vehicle owners) — all score Low due to absent or outdated primary sources. The market sizing claims are uniformly Low (aggregator research cluster, APAC-as-proxy). Importantly, no claim reaches High confidence; the strongest individual claims (TIA fraud report data, BSI/TT Club theft data) reach only Medium because they each appear as single sources. The stage does not qualify for ship-as-is. Remediation is targeted and achievable: the five weak claims identified for deep-research collectively require fetching 4–6 primary sources (CargoNet/Verisk annual theft statistics, ATRI nuclear verdict report, BPS Indonesia transport stats, TT Club PDF verification of the 1,475% figure, and one independent broker workflow survey). With those additions, the pct-Low would drop below 50% and the most critical cost and frequency claims would reach Medium or High. The SEA market sizing gap (geography mismatch) is a structural limitation that cannot be remediated from web sources alone and should be flagged for primary interview or ADB/World Bank SEA logistics report sourcing.
